Testimony ofSenator Anne Carney introducing
LD 457, An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects Related to the Repair of Campus
Infrastructure Used for Active Transportation and Outdoor Recreation before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs March 3, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Warren, and esteemed colleagues on the Cormnittee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, I am Senator Anne Carney, proudly representing Senate District 29, which
includes South Portland, Cape Elizabeth and part of Scarborough. It is a pleasure to be with you
today to introduce LD 457, "An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects Related to the Repair of
Campus Infrastructure Used for Active Transportation and Outdoor Recreation."
This legislation, if passed, will invest $1 million in climate resiliency projects to repair historic
structures on the campus of Southern Maine Community College, especially those used by members of the community for active transportation and outdoor recreation. The goal is to repair and restore
Fort Preble and the trails which run over it. What I found in my quest to help SMCC and our
community repair the damage caused by last winter's storms is that most of our grant opportunities exclude educational institutions from applying. This would create a new pathway to fund these
important repairs.
Portland Harbor has long been the maritime hub of our state, since even before Maine became independent from Massachusetts. Fort Preble was built in 1807 on the northeastern shore of what was then Cape Elizabeth to help protect our nation's nascent economy by enforcing the 1807 Embargo Act, which prohibited American cargo ships from trading with the British and French.
Fort Preble then served an important naval purpose to help defend Portland Harbor in the War of 1812, the Civil War, and all the way through World War II. During this final war, it was especially
crucial in protecting the Todd-Bath Iron Shipbuilding Corporation shipyard next door as Mainers
made a crucial contribution to the war effort by constructing hundreds of Liberty Ships for the U.S.
Navy.
The military decommissioned Fort Preble in 1950, and the State of Maine transferred it shortly thereafter to the institution which would become Southern Maine Community College. The college has stewarded this landmark, and the trails that run over and around it, for the decades since, helping to preserve its history and maintain open access for students, visitors, and the South Portland community.

1

Unfortunately, last winter's storms interrupted that access by undermining the structural integrity of
this centuries-old fort, and indeed the whole eastern coast of the SMCC campus. In order to keep the public and its employees safe, SMCC made the tough decision to fence off access to the fort and
some of its trails. This decision disappointed many in the community, but it is understandable given
that the full extent of the damage to Fort Preble and the SMCC's coastal infrastructure is still
unknown.
SMCC needs to conduct an engineering study to understand the scope of the threat and what Work
must be done to fix the damage in a cost-effective and enduring manner. Unfortunately, just the
study costs over $100,000, not to mention the repairs themselves, which could total in the millions once the fort, the trails, and academic and administrative buildings are included.
This legislation will help to cover the cost of this undertaking, seeking to work in partnership with private, local, and potentially federal funding. This bill will not be a panacea for Fort Preble or the academic infrastructure which surrounds it, given the constantly growing threats posed by climate change, sea level rise, and strengthening storms, but it is a necessary investment in coastal resilience
for a vital educational institution in our state.
It would also go a long way to restore and protect access to trails and coastal infrastructure used for
recreation and active transportation, as the Spring Point Shoreway passes over Fort Preble on its
way to CO1'1I16C'[ Willard Beach with Bug Light Park and the South Portland Greenbelt. These trails are part of what makes South Portland a walkable and active coastal community, and it is important for us to come together to invest in their future.
I'll close by sharing a personal story about Fort Preble and this section of coastline. Some of you
may know that cycling is a passion of mine. One of my favorite routes is what I like to call the "Tour de District 29." I leave from my house in Cape Elizabeth, pass by Two Lights (Cape
Elizabeth Light), head up Shore Road to Portland Head Light, continue out to Willard Beach, take the Spring Point Shoreway up over Fort Preble to get to Spring Point Ledge Light, and then spend some time at Bug Light appreciating the Liberty Ship memorial and the significant contribution our
community and state made to the victory in WWII as a result of the dedication of all who worked to build the Liberty Ships. I then head west on the Eastern Trail and make my way to Scarborough
Beach and then Higgins Beach before heading home on Route 77. Each of these scenic areas received heavy damage last winter. The storms and the resulting damage can still be seen along the
"Tour de SD 29." In particular, the washout forced the closure of the Shoreway along Fort Preble,
and the damage will endure without an investment of resources. I believe that with some resources for at least an engineering study, the community, alums and others who enjoy the Shoreway will
step up to support restoration and reopening of this section of the SMCC campus and the Shoreway.
I hope you will join me in supporting this investment in our coastal recreational and educational
infrastructure.
Thank you for allowing me the opportunity to introduce this bill. I welcome any questions you may
have.
Anne Carney
State Senator, District 29

FROM: David Daigler, President, Maine Community College System

Testimony Neither For Nor Against LD 457 An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects

DATE: March 3, 2025

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, I am David Daigler, President of the Maine Community College System and I am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 457. I would like to start by saying that I appreciate
Senator Carney's dedication to her community and her constituents and her willingness to work with us
as she crafted this legislation.
We are here neither for nor against LD 457 because as you well know, the Maine Community College
System has three funding priorities this session: an increase to our base budget, support for the Maine Free College initiative, along with language to ensure it becomes an ongoing program, and funds for our share of the newly established paid family medical leave program. All three of these initiatives directly impact our ability to fulfill our statutory obligation to train and educate Maine's workforce. All three allow us to serve thousands of Maine residents across the state as well as work to compensate our employees for their hard work and dedication.
Having said that, no one is more devastated than the SMCC and MCCS communities when winter storm after winter storm batter the edges of the stunning SMCC campus. As some of you know, I am an avid
biker and can often be found on the Greenbelt Walkway.
We also do not want chain-link fences blocking access to community members who use the beltway to
commute, walk, enjoy the view or grieve a loved one.

As soon as the gravity of the damage to the edges of our campus came to light after the December 2023 storm, we went to work. First, we assured that no one would get injured on unstable ground (hence the chain link fences and no trespassing signs). Then we started to look at funding opportunities to do our
best to mitigate further damage and allow public access. However, as I said at the beginning of my
testimony, our first responsibility is to educate Maine's workforce. Erosion at SMCC does not only
affect the beautiful greenway but also threatens some of our most critical educational buildings.
Therefore, any fundraising that is done by MCCS for the Greenbelt cannot be at the expense of our
mission and needs to focus on our crumbling infrastructure.
Unfortunately, rising sea levels and climate change will continue to hammer our coastline. This means,
we don't get to rebuild Fort Preble as it was. We will have to shore it up and hope to mitigate future
damage.
As you heard from Dr. Miller, we are working to evaluate the options with the hopes that community members and other funders who focus on historic preservation or recreation will take a lead in this
effort.
We really do appreciate Senator Carney's work and, of course, the funds provided in this bill would be
welcome and used, as we use all of our funds, efficiently and for their intended purpose.
Thank you.
10034992: 160 Fort Road South Portland, Maine 04106 March 1, 2025 To the members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee Public Hearing on Monday, March 3, 2025,10am I write to you today in support of the bill LD457, An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects Related to the Repair of Campus Infrastructure Used for Active Transportation and Outdoor Recreation" I arrived on the campus of SMVTI in the fall of 1976 to study Applied Marine Biology and have never left. FROM: Dr. Kristen Miller, President, Southern Maine Community College

RE:

Testimony Neither For Nor Against LD 457, An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects
Related to the Repair of Campus Infrastructure Used for Active Transportation and
Outdoor Recreation

DATE: March 3, 2025

Thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
SMCC's waterfront campus is not only a vital educational institution but also home to a historic and scenic
landscape that is deeply valued by the community. However, the devastation from recent storms has severely impacted our coastline, causing significant damage to the greenbelt, Fort Preble, and other public areas. More critically, the erosion threatens key educational facilities that serve our students and support Maine's workforce development. Rising sea levels and climate change continue to pose a growing risk, and without strategic investments, the long-term sustainability of both our campus and its historic landmarks remains uncertain.

We are actively evaluating options to ensure our facilities remain intact and to implement measures that
protect against future erosion. However, our ability to fund repairs and long-term mitigation for Fort Preble and the greenbelt would significantly impact our budget and our capacity to invest in solutions for
our educational infrastructure. To address this challenge, we are working with community members, the
City of South Portland, and other organizations to explore partnerships for fundraising and support. While
we are committed to being part of the solution, SMCC cannot lead this effort alone, as our primary
responsibility remains providing high-quality education and workforce training to Maine residents.

In response, SMCC has taken immediate action to ensure public safety by securing unstable areas while working to preserve access to the greenbelt and Fort Preble. We recognize the historical and cultural
significance of this site and remain committed to maintaining public access. At the same time, we must
prioritize our core mission of educating Maine's workforce, ensuring that any fundraising or restoration efforts do not come at the expense of our students, faculty, or essential campus infrastructure.

We appreciate Senator Carney's leadership in bringing attention to this issue and welcome discussions on
how best to preserve and enhance public access. However, as we move forward, it is critical that we seek
long-term solutions that address both the preservation of this historic site and the protection of our
educational facilities--ensuring that SMCC can continue to serve students and the broader community for
generations to come.

Thank you for your time, I am happy to take any questions.

March 3, 2025 Honorable Chair and Members of the Committee: I am Natalie West. I serve as an at large member of the South Portland City Council. I speak today as an individual Council member in support of LD 457. My remarks are focused specifically on the importance of repairing or relocating the Spring Point Shoreway Trail, which was significantly damaged by the 2024 storms.
I am confident that your investment in this trail will eventually be repaid from increased revenues generated by those who use the trail. To explain in more detail, the Shoreway Trail follows the waterfront for approximately � mile through the campus of Southern Maine Community College along one of the most scenic and easily accessible portions of our coast. There is a photo with approximate location of the trail shown on my written testimony. (see below.) From the trail, there are views of lighthouses, islands, lobster boats, forts - and ship traffic coming and going to Portland Harbor. The Shoreway Trail has it all. It also links to our regional Greenbelt Pathway, which in turn becomes the Eastern Trail, extending 65 miles to the South.
In addition to its natural beauty, this one-half mile of improved paved trail has historic significance. It connects South Portland landmarks that span almost 400 years of Maine History - starting with the lighthouse in Buglight Park, past the memorial to the Liberty Ships built in World War II, through Fort Preble (built in 1808) and Old Settlers Cemetery (dating from 1658), to Willard Beach - a public beach, which in turn leads to Fisherman's Point, part of the King's Highway, constructed in the 1650's.
Because the trail is paved, it can be used almost year-round, by pedestrians, bicyclists, families with strollers. Portions of it are accessible to those in wheelchairs or using other mobility aids.
Because of its accessibility, scenic qualities and historic importance, the trail heavily used by visitors who patronize our restaurants, shops and lodging opportunities, which supports and strengthens the economic base of our region. I urge your support of LD 457.

Re: Testimony in support of LD457, An Act to Fund Climate Resiliency Projects Related to the Repair of Campus Infrastructure Used for Active Transportation and Outdoor Recreation
Chairman Rafferty, Chairwoman Murphy and distinguished members of the Committee; Thank you for the opportunity to offer comments in support of LD457.
My name is Scott Morelli and I am the City Manager of South Portland, Maine. Our
city has been collaborating with Southern Maine Community College to maintain a publicly accessible trail system around Spring Point, the location of historic Fort
Preble on the SMCC Campus. The fort is not only an historic asset of the State of
Maine and the City of South Portland, but is a popular landmark at the gateway and
entry point to Portland Harbor.
In recent years, we have witnessed successive storms batter the fort and portions of the historic structure have fallen into the sea. Without an immediate intervention, we
fear the fort will eventually be lost in a matter of years. The college has invested its
own resources into stabilizing the structure to mitigate further damage and protect the public. However, the college is constrained for resources and we all must
acknowledge that this effort is well outside their core mission to educate and train our future workforce.
A more deliberate intervention is needed, which requires dedicated resources that leverage additional investment from private donations and federal grants for a more
lasting solution. This funding will ensure the fort is properly stabilized and protected,
and repairs can be made. Although climate change may result in more intense storms in the years ahead, there are modern techniques to stabilize and repair historic stone structures that will go a long way to protect this investment in historic preservation
and maintaining the area for the pub|ic's continued use and enjoyment.
Respectfully submitted,
Scott Morelli
